Action Plan:
1) Refer urgently to a Mini-Stroke/TIA clinic today to evaluate suspected transient ischemic attack/ischemic event and to exclude stroke. The clinic will perform carotid ultrasound and brain imaging (and other appropriate tests) as part of a rapid assessment; expect contact within 1–2 days for an appointment.
2) If symptoms recur, worsen, or persist, proceed to the emergency department (A&E) promptly. Provide patient with PALS and TIA clinic contact numbers and instructions to call to confirm scheduling; ask patient to self-monitor and seek urgent care if deficits develop.
3) Documentation and follow-up: Referral placed and notes with clinic contact details left in the chart; patient advised to call to confirm slot and to report any recurrence or new symptoms.
4) Verbal consent from patient has been obtained before using transcription software.

Note: A COVID-19 vaccine suitability assessment was not documented as part of this visit.

Subjective:
- Presenting complaint: About 6–8 weeks of very unusual, episodic neurological symptoms.
- Symptoms and progression:
  - Right hand numbness/tingling (paresthesias) with episodes of right arm weakness.
  - Right leg weakness and a slightly abnormal gait during episodes.
  - Fatigue and nausea ongoing over the month.
  - Difficulty with tasks during episodes (e.g., cannot hold a cup; drinking coffee more difficult during episodes; sensation of something in the throat but able to speak).
  - Episodes started about 6–8 weeks ago, lasted several days (roughly 3–4 days) and have become more frequent (from about weekly to a couple of times per day).
  - No current symptoms at the time of this visit.
  - No clear visual changes or speech difficulty reported during episodes; able to speak during episodes.
- Past medical history: No chronic illnesses described; prior screening for diabetes, blood pressure, and cholesterol reportedly normal.
- Medications: Aspirin 75 mg daily (self-initiated to reduce stroke risk); route not documented.
- Allergies: Penicillin.
- Social history: Works as a plastic surgeon; lives with wife; non-smoker.
- Family history: Father had carotid surgery to reduce stroke risk; no personal history of stroke or TIAs reported.
- ROS/information gathered: No current swallowing difficulty; no persistent vision changes; no current focal deficits.

Objective:
- No vitals or formal physical examination findings documented.
- Neurological exam not performed or not recorded in this encounter.
- Video connection interrupted; doctor proceeded with verbal assessment.
- Prior labs: Diabetes, blood pressure, and cholesterol previously checked and reported normal.

Assessment & Plan:
1) Suspected transient ischemic attack / ischemic cerebrovascular event (TIA/stroke):
   - Assessment: Working diagnosis = TIA/stroke (high likelihood per transcript and DDx guidance); consistent with episodic, unilateral right-sided numbness/weakness and gait change with increasing frequency.
   - Differential diagnoses from DDx (consistent with transcript; note conflict noted):
     - Relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (MS) – medium likelihood.
     - Migraine with aura – medium likelihood.
     - Brain tumor or other structural lesion – low–medium likelihood.
     - Vitamin B12 deficiency neuropathy – low likelihood.
     - Cervical artery dissection / vascular anomaly – low likelihood.
     - Autoimmune/inflammatory processes (e.g., CNS vasculitis) – low likelihood.
     - Traumatic cervical or vascular injury – low likelihood.
     - Endocrine/metabolic causes (e.g., hypoglycemia) – low likelihood.
   - Investigations planned:
     - Urgent referral to TIA clinic with vascular imaging (carotid ultrasound) and brain imaging to rule out stroke/TIA and carotid disease.
     - Additional tests as indicated by the clinic (e.g., brain MRI/CT, further vascular studies).
   - Treatment planned:
     - No acute therapy started today; definitive management and further workup in the TIA clinic.
     - Education on red-flag symptoms and ED redirection if symptoms recur or worsen.
   - Referrals:
     - Referral to TIA/mini-stroke clinic placed; instructions to contact and attend promptly.
     - If needed, patient may be contacted by the clinic with scheduling; numbers for PALS and clinic provided in notes.
   - Follow-up: Patient to monitor symptoms; return or present to ED if deficits persist or worsen; clinic scheduling to be confirmed.
   
Quality checks (document and process considerations):
- Missing elements clinically expected for a consult:
  - No documented vital signs or formal neurological examination.
  - No current medication reconciliation beyond aspirin; other meds not detailed.
  - No imaging or laboratory results obtained during this visit.
- Internal conflicts between transcript and DDx:
  - Conflict noted: Transcript describes episodes lasting several days with recovery between events, whereas some DDx items (e.g., TIAs) are typically acute events; a discrepancy noted between observed presentation and DDx expectations.
- Transcript quality:
  - Video connection issues; audio quality intermittently affected; partial limitations in physical exam data due to remote encounter. No major data loss beyond lack of in-person exam.

Notes for clinician:
- Emphasize urgent evaluation for potential TIAs given focal right-sided symptoms, gait disturbance, and family history.
- Ensure patient understands the urgency and adheres to the rapid clinic scheduling, with clear red-flag guidance for ED if symptoms recur.
- Consider full medication reconciliation at next visit, including aspirin rationale and risks.
